body: 2014 letter, 'Berkshire Today': 'Conglomerates ... have a terrible reputation with investors. And they richly deserve it.' The late-1960s drill: 'By personality, promotion or dubious accounting - and often by all three - these managers drove a fledgling conglomerate's stock to, say, 20 times earnings and then issued shares as fast as possible to acquire another business selling at ten-or-so times earnings. They immediately applied "pooling" accounting to the acquisition, which - with not a dime's worth of change in the underlying businesses - automatically increased per-share earnings, and used the rise as proof of managerial genius.' The game needs an ever-rising stock price and ends when it stops. Same letter credits Munger's blueprint: 'Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices.' Berkshire's own rule (1983/1989): issue stock only 'when we receive as much in intrinsic business value as we give.' Actionable red flag for Indian markets: serial acquirers or roll-ups paying with richly valued paper or QIP money, rising EPS mostly from acquisitions, goodwill growing faster than operating cash flow, frequent restatements/segment changes. Test: organic growth and cash conversion excluding acquisitions.
title: Buffett 2014: how high-P/E acquirers manufacture EPS growth - the 1960s conglomerate drill

body: Two contradictory base rates, both true for their window. (1) 2010-2021: ThePrint (May 2022) - shares of about half the PSUs that went public since 2010 traded below IPO price; Quartz (2019) - eight of ten government firms listed since 2017 had lost investors money. PSU IPOs were priced for disinvestment targets, and LIC (May 2022) listed at Rs867 vs Rs949 issue. (2) 2020-2025: a PTI analysis (Apr 2025) found IPO investors in 15 of 18 CPSEs listed over eight years earned 'bumper' gains: Mazagon Dock (2020 issue Rs145) ~+3,700%; RVNL (2019, ~Rs19) ~+1,866%; IRCTC (2019, Rs320) ~+1,110% (only PSU IPO listing at >100% premium); Garden Reach >1,000%; IRFC (2021, Rs26) ~Rs142 in Apr 2025. Laggards were insurers - LIC below issue; GIC Re and New India Assurance negative even after 2018 1:1 bonuses. Drivers of the turn: defence indigenisation and rail capex budgets, dividend yields of 5-8% at 2020-21 lows, single-digit P/Es, then retail/thematic-fund flows. Lesson: ownership type is not destiny; starting valuation + policy tailwind + order book visibility drove returns. Early signal visible in 2020-21: PSU P/E and P/B at multi-decade lows while government capex and import substitution policy were explicit. Risk on the other side: 2024 peak valuations (40-60x P/E for some defence/rail names) reversed sharply. Figures are dated snapshots (2019-2025), adjust for splits/bonuses before reuse.
title: PSU IPOs in India: poor for a decade, then a 2020-24 rerating made them the best IPO cohort - regime, not structure

body: After the Feb-2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling, US importers booked refunds, usually as a COGS credit, and stripped them out of adjusted numbers. (1) The refund ÷ direct-import FOB (purchases × import share ÷ (1 + rate)) gives the effective tariff rate borne. Five Below: $163.6M on ~40% direct imports ≈ 20-22% effective. (2) GAAP EPS and GAAP gross margin are distorted for four quarters (FIVE Q2 FY26 GAAP GM 48.5% vs adjusted 35.6%), so screens on trailing GAAP numbers mislead. (3) Goods bought from domestic vendors carried tariffs inside the vendor price. Those refunds go to the vendor, not the retailer. Ask whether vendors pass any back. Nobody asked this on the call. (4) Check how the proxy's PSU metric treats the refund.
title: A tariff refund booked in COGS reveals the tariff cost actually borne; split importer-of-record from domestic-vendor exposure
